newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG army chief agrees to stand down, urges restraint.
newsitem.headline: PNG army chief agrees to stand down, urges restraint.

text.p: The Papua New Guinea army chief who sparked a crisis by demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan agreed on Tuesday to accept his own sacking, a senior aide said.

The aide said defence force commander Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok, who turned against Chan on Monday over a plan to use foreign mercenaries to quash an island uprising, was only waiting for official notice of his dismissal.
But it was unclear if Singirok's departure would spell an end to the crisis in the South Pacific nation or if he would continue his bitter campaign against the prime minister.
The streets of Port Moresby were calm but tense as army and police force waited for the standoff to be resolved.
"The commander is still waiting for the official writs to come down from the governor-general's office," Lieutenant-Colonel Joseph Fabila, a Singirok aide, told Reuters.
"He will then stand down and he then plans to hold an official press conference some time after he receives the official writs."

Fabila, speaking from the central barracks where Singirok is holed up, said Singirok had again urged restraint on his troops. "He is going to allow the normal democratic and constitutional processes to occur and he is pleading to the public and the troops to exercise restraint and to go about their normal activities," he said.

Singirok brought about the young nation's worst political crisis in 22 years of independence on Monday when he called on Chan and other ministers to resign within 48 hours or be forced out of office by his people.

Officials said on Tuesday that senior PNG legal figures were meeting to discuss what charges might be brought against the 40-year-old Australian-trained soldier, who has denied mounting any sort of coup.

Singirok turned against Chan over his decision to hire foreign soldiers of fortune, mostly from Africa, to help quell a nine-year-old secessionist struggle on resource-rich Bougainville, 900 kms (560 miles) northeast of the capital.
Monday's uncertainty sent the shares of major investors in the country downwards, although PNG stocks listed on the Australian stock exchange began to recover ground on Tuesday.
Chan, who has the support of the country's powerful police force, ordered late on Monday that Singirok be replaced by little-known Colonel Alfred Aikung.
Australia, a close neighbour, has expressed its concern over the crisis. Canberra has argued strongly against the use of mercenaries but says PNG's constitution must be respected.
New Zealand foreign minister Don McKinnon said he hoped the crisis would now subside and all sides could go on to tackle the Bougainville conflict through negotiation.
"It's going to take a few more days and some cool heads must prevail," McKinnon told New Zealand radio on Tuesday.
"We've taken the stand that there has to be a political solution to this particular problem at Bougainville. It can't be a military solution."

Much of the fighting on the island has centred around the giant Panguna copper-gold mine, owned 53.6 percent by global mining giant RTZ Corp Plc-CRA Ltd. The mine closed in 1989 at the start of the uprising.
The mine had contributed much-needed foreign capital to Papua New Guinea, which relies on exports of crude oil, gold, timber, copper and coffee for its per capita gross domestic product of US$1,228.
